## Simple explanation

A decision tree makes a prediction by asking a series of questions about
input features. Each answer follows a branch until the example reaches a
leaf containing a prediction.

## Technical explanation

At each internal node, a tree selects a feature and split that improves a
criterion such as impurity reduction. Leaves return class labels,
probabilities, or numeric values. Depth limits and pruning help control
overfitting; exact criteria differ across implementations.

## Why it matters in AI engineering

Decision trees are relatively easy to inspect and can model nonlinear
relationships without requiring feature scaling. They provide useful
baselines, though deep trees can be unstable and may generalize poorly.

## How it works

Training recursively partitions examples based on feature tests. The
algorithm chooses splits that make resulting groups more homogeneous
according to its objective. Prediction follows the learned tests from the
root to a leaf.

## Practical example

A simple tree predicting whether a transaction needs review might split
first on transaction amount, then on account age, and assign a risk class
at each leaf.

## Common misconceptions

- A tree diagram is not necessarily a faithful or complete explanation
  when it is very large or part of an ensemble.
- A shallow tree is interpretable only if its features and thresholds are
  meaningful and understood.
- Decision trees do not automatically handle every missing value or
  categorical feature in the same way.
